step_by_step_reasoning: The whiteboard shows Snap's send/receive snap platform on AWS. The 10 inventory entities are kept as 10 nodes: the two mobile icons are distinct (iOS sender, Android recipient), and the four EKS workloads (Media, MCS, Friend Graph, SnapDB) perform distinct steps, so they are not fused. The gateway (GW) drawn on the board and mentioned in the audio is not in the authoritative entity inventory, and ledger edges cannot be re-routed, so it is recorded only in notes. Flow 0 (send snap): iOS -> Media -> CloudFront -> S3 to persist the media; iOS -> MCS; MCS <-> Friend Graph for the permission check; MCS -> SnapDB -> DynamoDB to persist metadata, with the return edges DynamoDB -> SnapDB -> MCS. Flow 1 (receive snap): MCS -> ElastiCache lookup of connection/server ID, ElastiCache -> MCS result, MCS -> Android push over the persistent connection, and S3 -> CloudFront to serve the media by media ID. Self-check: visual_connections has 14 entries and 14 edges are emitted, one per entry with the same source and target, including all reverse directions. No edges were added beyond the ledger.

graph.name: Snap: Sending and Receiving a Snap on AWS (EKS, DynamoDB, ElastiCache, CloudFront)
graph.notes: Snapchat platform on AWS. 300M+ daily active users, 5B+ snaps/day, 10M+ QPS. 900+ EKS clusters, many with 1,000+ instances. The new architecture reduced P50 send-snap latency by 24%. Compute cost is controlled with auto-scaling and Graviton instance types. Clients reach the EKS microservices through a custom-built gateway (GW) running on EKS.

nodes.name: iOS Client (Sender)
nodes.notes: Snapchat iOS app that sends the snap; talks to the backend through Snap's custom gateway (GW) built on EKS.

nodes.name: Android Client (Recipient)
nodes.notes: Recipient client; keeps a persistent connection to a gateway server so messages can be pushed quickly. Receiving is very latency sensitive.

nodes.name: Media Delivery Service
nodes.notes: EKS microservice for media delivery; sends the snap media to CloudFront and persists it in S3 so it is closer to the recipient.

nodes.name: MCS (Messaging Service)
nodes.notes: EKS messaging service; orchestrates the permission check, metadata persistence, connection lookup and push to the recipient. Part of 900+ EKS clusters, many with 1,000+ instances.

nodes.name: Friend Graph
nodes.notes: EKS microservice that checks whether the sender has permission to send snaps to the recipient.

nodes.name: SnapDB
nodes.notes: Snap's own database front end to DynamoDB running on EKS; implements transactions, TTL, efficient handling of ephemeral data and incremental state synchronization to reduce the load on DynamoDB and keep costs under control.

nodes.name: CloudFront
nodes.notes: Receives the snap media and serves it close to the recipient; media is fetched using the media ID.

nodes.name: ElastiCache
nodes.notes: Stores session metadata: connection ID / server ID of the persistent connection for each client; also holds the media ID.

nodes.name: DynamoDB
nodes.notes: Stores snap metadata (including media ID); 400 TB of data; nightly scans at 2 billion rows per minute for friend suggestions and deleting ephemeral data.

edges.notes: iOS app sends the snap media through the gateway (GW) to the media delivery service.
Media service sends the snap to CloudFront so it is closer to the recipient.
Snap media is persisted in S3.
iOS app sends the snap message through the gateway (GW) to the messaging service.
MCS asks Friend Graph whether the sender has permission to send snaps.
Friend Graph returns the permission check result.
MCS writes snap metadata (including media ID) to SnapDB.
SnapDB persists the metadata in DynamoDB.
SnapDB returns the result to the messaging service.
MCS looks up the connection ID / server ID of the recipient's persistent connection in ElastiCache.
ElastiCache returns the session metadata identifying the server the client is connected to.
MCS pushes the message to the recipient through the gateway server holding the persistent connection.
Media (image/video) is retrieved from S3 via CloudFront using the media ID.
